title: 5 Best Attending Physician Scheduling Software Tools Compared
description: QGenda, Amion, TigerConnect, spreadsheets and Scheduling Wizard compared for attending and faculty scheduling: who builds it, call fairness and admin burden.
content:
Summary

  • Building physician schedules eats hours every month for whoever owns it, and fairness matters: a published study of one residency found a rebuilt call schedule raised perceived fairness from 43% to 95%.
  • Most tools either publish the schedule, like Amion, or ask you to build it yourself in a platform like QGenda.
  • The critical choice for program coordinators is between software you must operate and a managed service that delivers a finished schedule.
  • For programs that want to hand off the administrative burden, a managed service like Scheduling Wizard builds the finished schedule for you, to your rules.

If you searched "attending physician scheduling software" and landed here, you've probably already noticed something frustrating: most search results return tools built for patient appointment booking, like online intake forms, patient portals, and calendar widgets for scheduling office visits. That's not what you need.

What you're looking for is physician workforce scheduling, the process of building Block rotation schedules, Call schedules, and Clinic assignments for a department, group or program, with the ACGME requirements in it where they apply.

These are different problems, and conflating them costs you time you don't have.

We should say up front that we are Scheduling Wizard, a service that builds physician schedules, and that we included ourselves here. Read our entry with that in mind. The list is ordered by who builds your group's attending schedule: a service first, the spreadsheet second, then software and the platforms you publish through. Sort by price or mobile app and the order would change. The other tools are described as their own users and documentation describe them.

What Physician Scheduling Costs the Person Who Owns It

Here is how one hospitalist described the work:

"It takes at least 4-8 hours a month to make the schedule… and that's before the swaps, tracking fairness, and just carrying it in your head all month. That's what really adds up.", r/hospitalist discussion

Time is only part of it. There is also the knowledge that leaves when the person who built the schedule moves on. It's the ACGME duty hour violations that get caught only after the schedule is already published. Then there's the morale hit when physicians feel the call schedule isn't fair.

That last point matters more than most administrators realize: a study in Neurosurgery found that rebuilding the call schedule to written rules boosted residents' perceived fairness of the call schedule from 43% to 95%.

What an Attending Schedule Has to Balance

Attending and faculty schedules have different rules from resident schedules, and they are often harder to agree on because the people being scheduled are also the people who decide the rules.

  • Clinical effort and contracts. Each physician has a contracted clinical effort, and some have protected time for research, teaching or administration. The schedule has to match those commitments over the year, not just week to week.
  • Call and weekend equity. Nights, weekends and holidays need to even out across partners or faculty over a year, by whatever definition of fair the group has agreed.
  • Coverage across sites and services. Many groups cover more than one hospital, clinic or service line, each with its own minimums.
  • Supervision of trainees. Where residents or fellows are involved, the attending schedule has to provide the supervision their programs require, so the two schedules depend on each other.
  • Leave and requests. Vacation, conferences and personal requests have to be handled consistently, because inconsistency is what starts disputes in a group.

The ACGME work hour limits apply to residents and fellows, not to attendings, so an attending schedule is built to the group's own rules. Those rules are rarely written down in full, which is why building it usually starts with writing them down.

How We Evaluated These Tools

We compared each option on the same five questions:

  • Who Builds It: Does it generate schedules, or just publish them?
  • Call Fairness Distribution: Is fairness built in, or manually tracked?
  • Custom rules: Can it handle GME-specific rules and cross-schedule dependencies?
  • ACGME/Credentialing Compliance: Does it prevent violations, or flag them after the fact?
  • Administrative Burden: How much time and expertise does it require from your team?

Here are five options for attending physician scheduling: a managed service, the spreadsheet, two scheduling platforms and a publishing platform.

1. Scheduling Wizard (Managed Service, Not Software)

Best for: departments, provider groups and training programs that want the build off their plate entirely.

Scheduling Wizard is the one managed service on this list. It's a done-for-you managed scheduling service backed by Y Combinator (W26), built for GME programs, provider groups and practices. Instead of handing you a platform to learn and configure, we write your rules down with you and deliver finished schedules as Excel or Google Sheets, or on a custom live view we build for you.

You submit your rules (vacation requests, rotation requirements, coverage rules, resident preferences) and receive the finished block, call, clinic and attending schedules, built to your rules. There is nothing for your team to configure or learn.

Rubric What to expect
Who Builds It Fully managed, zero software to operate
Call Fairness Distribution Built for fair call, weekend, and holiday distribution
Custom rules Cross-schedule dependencies resolved in the build
ACGME Compliance Built to the requirements you tell us apply; the final review is a check, not a repair job
Administrative Burden Minimal, you send rules and review the result

The other difference is continuity. When your chief resident or scheduling lead moves on, the written-down rules stay with us, so the next person does not start from scratch.

Where the schedule lives is entirely up to you. Programs that already use Amion or QGenda for day-to-day viewing often upload our finished schedule into it; others use the live view, or both.

What you get: the finished schedule as an Excel or Google Sheets file, or on a custom live view we build for the group. Redrafts come with it: when a partner's availability changes or a site shifts its coverage, we rebuild rather than hand you a correction exercise. For the specifics, see our page on attending physician scheduling.

2. Excel / Google Sheets

Best for: Groups whose coverage rules and contract terms change faster than a platform can be reconfigured.

A lot of attending coverage is still built in spreadsheets, including at some departments that own an enterprise platform. That is why it is second. A spreadsheet takes contract terms, site splits, partner preferences and the handshake agreements that never got written down, and it takes them immediately. Sheets lets the whole group see the same version.

The trade is that fairness is whatever the person counting says it is. Call equity across a year is an arithmetic problem, and arithmetic done by hand under time pressure is where disputes start.

3. QGenda

Best for: Large health systems with dedicated administrative staff and IT resources.

QGenda is a well-known name in physician workforce management. It's a complete, enterprise-grade SaaS platform that goes beyond scheduling to include credentialing, time tracking, and analytics, all in one system.

But "complete" comes with a caveat. As one physician put it in an online forum: "Getting QG to actually do what you want isn't easy, and learning how it works is very complicated." QGenda does a lot, and it works best with an administrator who has the time to configure and maintain it.

Rubric What to expect
Who Builds It Self-service, rules and templates must be built and managed by your team
Call Fairness Distribution Trackable; depends on how the rules are configured
Custom rules Flexible; complex GME rules are configured by your team
ACGME Compliance Rules configured by your team; someone still reviews the output
Administrative Burden Training and ongoing maintenance on your side

QGenda makes the most sense for large health systems that have the administrative bandwidth to manage the platform and want a single integrated tool for all workforce operations. For an already-stretched chief resident or program coordinator, it can become another burden rather than a relief.

4. Amion

Best for: Programs that need a simple way to publish and share a finished schedule.

Amion is familiar across academic medicine, and it helps to be clear about what it is for. Amion is a schedule publishing platform, not a schedule generation tool. You build the schedule somewhere else (usually Excel), then input it into Amion so your physicians can view it from their phones or computers.

There's nothing wrong with that. For what it does, Amion does it well. But it does not reduce the core administrative burden of creating a fair, finished schedule; that work still happens entirely outside the platform.

Rubric What to expect
Who Builds It The program, before the schedule is published
Call Fairness Distribution Handled where the schedule is built
Custom rules Handled where the schedule is built
ACGME Compliance Handled where the schedule is built
Administrative Burden Low for publishing tasks, but does not address the burden of building the schedule

Amion is the last mile of the workflow: it is how people see the schedule. Many programs use it in combination with a creation tool or service.

5. TigerConnect Physician Scheduling

Best for: Hospitals already using TigerConnect for clinical communication.

TigerConnect is primarily known as a clinical communication and collaboration (CC&C) platform for secure messaging, alerts, and care team coordination. Their physician scheduling module is an add-on that integrates directly with that communication layer, meaning on-call notifications and schedule updates flow into the same system your team already uses for messaging.

As a standalone attending physician scheduling software, it's a capable self-service tool with rule-based automation and shift-request management. Like QGenda, the configuration and maintenance sit with your administrator.

Rubric What to expect
Who Builds It Self-service with rule-based draft generation, requires administrator management
Call Fairness Distribution Trackable, but dependent on careful and accurate user configuration
Custom rules Rule-based; configured by your team
ACGME Compliance Rules configured by your team; someone still reviews the output
Administrative Burden Moderate to high, requires learning the platform and managing ongoing scheduling

If your organization is already embedded in the TigerConnect ecosystem, the scheduling module is a natural fit. If you are not on TigerConnect already, compare it on how much of the build your team would still do.

The Decision Guide: Software to Run, or a Schedule That's Done?

The options here fall into four groups, and the right one depends on who you want doing the build.

Spreadsheets (Excel, Google Sheets): Flexible and familiar, with every hour of the build and every fairness count done by hand. Publishing platforms (Amion): Necessary for communicating a finished schedule to your team. Not useful for building one. If you already have a schedule creation process and just need a clean way to publish it, Amion is your answer.

Self-Service Platforms (QGenda, TigerConnect): These put a capable system in your hands, and learning, configuring and maintaining it falls on your chief resident or coordinator. These tools work well when you have dedicated administrative staff with the time and expertise to manage them. Many residency programs do not have that.

Managed Service (Scheduling Wizard): This is the only model where the operator burden leaves the program. You send your rules and get the finished schedule back, built to them, with no software to learn. When your chief rotates out, the institutional knowledge stays with the service.

In short:

If you need a tool to publish and share a schedule you've already built, use Amion or QGenda.

If you need someone to actually build the schedule for you, to your rules, Scheduling Wizard is the only managed service on this list.

Frequently Asked Questions

What's the difference between physician workforce scheduling and patient scheduling software?

Physician workforce scheduling software is designed to build complex staff schedules based on rules and requests, while patient scheduling software is for booking patient appointments. The tools you need for building a fair call schedule for dozens of residents, to the ACGME rules, are different from a calendar widget that lets a patient book an office visit online.

How does a managed service like Scheduling Wizard differ from software like QGenda?

A managed scheduling service builds the schedule for you and delivers a finished product, while scheduling software gives your team a tool to learn, configure and operate. The managed service model takes that work off your team.

How do I keep a residency schedule inside the ACGME rules?

Put the rules into the schedule while it is built, rather than flagging violations after a schedule exists. The review at the end then has far less to find.

How does Scheduling Wizard handle complex ACGME rules for specific subspecialties?

Scheduling Wizard handles subspecialty-specific ACGME rules by having our schedulers write your program’s rules down and build to them. Whether it's the supervision and case requirements in surgery, the clinic demands of internal medicine, or call frequency rules for anesthesiology, the requirements you tell us apply are part of the build.

Can I use Scheduling Wizard if my program already uses Amion?

Yes. It is entirely up to your group. We deliver the finished attending schedule as Excel or Google Sheets, or on a custom live view we build for you. Many groups keep Amion for daily viewing and upload our schedules straight into it; others use the live view, or both.

What happens when our chief resident leaves? How is scheduling knowledge retained?

Managed scheduling services solve the institutional continuity problem by keeping your program's rules, preferences and scheduling history written down with the service. When a chief resident rotates out, the knowledge of how to build your complex schedule doesn't leave with them. The new chief starts from a written rule set and last year's schedule rather than from a blank sheet.
